senses.d: O, the fifteenth letter of the English alphabet, derives its form, value, and name from the Greek O, through the Latin. The letter came into the Greek from the Phœnician, which possibly derived it ultimately from the Egyptian. Etymologically, the letter o is most closely related to a, e, and u; as in E. bone, AS. bān; E. stone, AS. stān; E. broke, AS. brecan to break; E. bore, AS. beran to bear; E. dove, AS. dūfe; E. toft, tuft; tone, tune; number, F. nombre.
Among the ancients, O was a mark of triple time, from the notion that the ternary, or number 3, is the most perfect of numbers, and properly expressed by a circle, the most perfect figure.
The letter O, or its sound.
Something shaped like the letter O; a circle or oval.
A cipher; zero.
q: Thou art an O without a figure.

senses.d: One.
An exclamation used in calling or directly addressing a person or personified object; also, as an emotional or impassioned exclamation expressing pain, grief, surprise, desire, fear, etc.
q: For ever, O Lord, thy word is settled in heaven.
O how love I thy law ! it is my meditation all the day.
O for a kindling touch from that pure flame !
But she is in her grave, — and oh The difference to me !
Oh for a lodge in some vast wilderness !
We should distinguish between the sign of the vocative and the emotional interjection, writing O for the former, and oh for the latter.

senses.d: Any tree or shrub of the genus Quercus. The oaks have alternate leaves, often variously lobed, and staminate flowers in catkins. The fruit is a smooth nut, called an acorn, which is more or less inclosed in a scaly involucre called the cup or cupule. There are now recognized about three hundred species, of which nearly fifty occur in the United States, the rest in Europe, Asia, and the other parts of North America, a very few barely reaching the northern parts of South America and Africa. Many of the oaks form forest trees of grand proportions and live many centuries. The wood is usually hard and tough, and provided with conspicuous medullary rays, forming the silver grain.
The strong wood or timber of the oak.

Oak.etym: [OE. oke, ok, ak, AS. āc; akin to D. eik, G. eiche, OHG. eih, Icel. eik, Sw. ek, Dan. eeg.]

senses.d: An implement for impelling a boat, being a slender piece of timber, usually ash or spruce, with a grip or handle at one end and a broad blade at the other. The part which rests in the rowlock is called the loom.
An oarsman; a rower; as, he is a good oar.
An oarlike swimming organ of various invertebrates.

Oar.etym: [AS. ār; akin to Icel. ār, Dan. aare, Sw. åra; perh. akin to E. row, v. Cf. Rowlock.]

senses.d: To row.
q: Oared with laboring arms.

senses.d: A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with a reverent appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
q: An oath of secrecy for the concealing of those which we think fit to keep secret.

senses.d: A solemn affirmation, connected with a sacred object, or one regarded as sacred, as the temple, the altar, the blood of Abel, the Bible, the Koran, etc.
An appeal (in verification of a statement made) to a superior sanction, in such a form as exposes the party making the appeal to an indictment for perjury if the statement be false.
A careless and blasphemous use of the name of the divine Being, or anything divine or sacred, by way of appeal or as a profane exclamation or ejaculation; an expression of profane swearing.

Oath.etym: [OE. othe, oth, ath, AS. āð; akin to D. eed, OS. ēð, G. eid, Icel. eiðr, Sw. ed, Dan. eed, Goth. aiþs; cf. OIr. oeth.]

senses.d: The act of obeying, or the state of being obedient; compliance with that which is required by authority; subjection to rightful restraint or control.
q: Government must compel the obedience of individuals.

senses.d: Words or actions denoting submission to authority; dutifulness.
A following; a body of adherents; as, the Roman Catholic obedience, or the whole body of persons who submit to the authority of the pope.

Obedience.etym: [F. obédience, L. obedientia, oboedientia. See Obedient, and cf. Obeisance.]

senses.d: Subject in will or act to authority; willing to obey; submissive to restraint, control, or command.
q: And floating straight, obedient to the stream.
The chief his orders gives; the obedient band, With due observance, wait the chief's command.

Obedient.etym: [OF. obedient, L. obediens, oboediens, -entis. p. pr. of obedire, oboedire, to obey. See Obey.]

senses.d: Obedience.
A manifestation of obedience; an expression of deference or respect; homage; a bow; a courtesy.
q: Bathsheba bowed and did obeisance unto the king.

Obeisance.etym: [F. obéissance obedience, fr. obéissant. See Obey, and cf. Obedience, Abaisance.]

senses.d: To give ear to; to execute the commands of; to yield submission to; to comply with the orders of.
q: Children, obey your parents in the Lord.
Was she the God, that her thou didst obey?

senses.d: To submit to the authority of; to be ruled by.
q: My will obeyed his will.
Afric and India shall his power obey.

senses.d: To yield to the impulse, power, or operation of; as, a ship obeys her helm.

Obey.etym: [OE. obeyen, F. obéir, fr. L. obedire, oboedire; ob (see Ob-) + audire to hear. See Audible, and cf. Obeisance.]

senses.d: To give obedience.
q: Will he obey when one commands?
His servants ye are, to whom ye obey.
He commanded the trumpets to sound: to which the two brave knights obeying, they performed their courses.

senses.d: To set before or against; to bring into opposition; to oppose.
q: Of less account some knight thereto object, Whose loss so great and harmful can not prove.
Some strong impediment or other objecting itself.
Pallas to their eyes The mist objected, and condensed the skies.

senses.d: To offer in opposition as a criminal charge or by way of accusation or reproach; to adduce as an objection or adverse reason.
q: He gave to him to object his heinous crime.
Others object the poverty of the nation.
The book . . . giveth liberty to object any crime against such as are to be ordered.

Object.etym: [L. objectus, p. p. of objicere, obicere, to throw or put before, to oppose; ob (see Ob-) + jacere to throw: cf. objecter. See Jet a shooting forth.]

senses.d: To make opposition in words or argument; — usually followed by to.

That which is put, or which may be regarded as put, in the way of some of the senses; something visible or tangible; as, he observed an object in the distance; all the objects in sight; he touched a strange object in the dark.

That which is set, or which may be regarded as set, before the mind so as to be apprehended or known; that of which the mind by any of its activities takes cognizance, whether a thing external in space or a conception formed by the mind itself; as, an object of knowledge, wonder, fear, thought, study, etc.
q: Object is a term for that about which the knowing subject is conversant; what the schoolmen have styled the “materia circa quam.”
The object of their bitterest hatred.

senses.d: That by which the mind, or any of its activities, is directed; that on which the purpose are fixed as the end of action or effort; that which is sought for; end; aim; motive; final cause.
q: Object, beside its proper signification, came to be abusively applied to denote motive, end, final cause . . . . This innovation was probably borrowed from the French.
Let our object be, our country, our whole country, and nothing but our country.

senses.d: Sight; show; appearance; aspect.
q: He, advancing close Up to the lake, past all the rest, arose In glorious object.

senses.d: A word, phrase, or clause toward which an action is directed, or is considered to be directed; as, the object of a transitive verb.
Opposed; presented in opposition; also, exposed.
The act of offering, or of making an offering.
Anything offered or presented in worship or sacred service; an offering; a sacrifice.
q: A peculiar . . . oblation given to God.
A pin was the usual oblation.

senses.d: A gift or contribution made to a church, as for the expenses of the eucharist, or for the support of the clergy and the poor.

Oblation.etym: [L. oblatio: cf. F. oblation. See Oblate.]

senses.d: Covered over, shaded, or darkened; destitute of light; imperfectly illuminated; dusky; dim.
q: His lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to darkness or night; inconspicuous to the sight; indistinctly seen; hidden; retired; remote from observation; unnoticed.
q: The obscure bird Clamored the livelong night.
The obscure corners of the earth.

senses.d: Not noticeable; humble; mean.
Not easily understood; not clear or legible; abstruse or blind; as, an obscure passage or inscription.
Not clear, full, or distinct; clouded; imperfect; as, an obscure view of remote objects.

Obscure.syn: Dark; dim; darksome; dusky; shadowy; misty; abstruse; intricate; difficult; mysterious; retired; unnoticed; unknown; humble; mean; indistinct.
Obscure.etym: [L. obscurus, orig., covered; ob- (see Ob-) + a root probably meaning, to cover; cf. L. scutum shield, Skr. sku to cover: cf. F. obscur. Cf. Sky.]

senses.d: To render obscure; to darken; to make dim; to keep in the dark; to hide; to make less visible, intelligible, legible, glorious, beautiful, or illustrious.
q: They are all couched in a pit hard by Herne's oak, with obscured lights.
Why, 't is an office of discovery, love, And I should be obscured.
There is scarce any duty which has been so obscured by the writings of learned men as this.
And seest not sin obscures thy godlike frame?

Obscure.etym: [L. obscurare, fr. obscurus: cf. OF. obscurer. See Obscure, a.]

senses.d: To conceal one's self; to hide; to keep dark.
q: How! There's bad news. I must obscure, and hear it.

senses.d: Obscurity.
The quality or state of being obscure; darkness; privacy; inconspicuousness; unintelligibleness; uncertainty.
q: You are not for obscurity designed.
They were now brought forth from obscurity, to be contemplated by artists with admiration and despair.

senses.d: The act or the faculty of observing or taking notice; the act of seeing, or of fixing the mind upon, anything.
q: My observation, which very seldom lies.

senses.d: The result of an act, or of acts, of observing; view; reflection; conclusion; judgment.
q: In matters of human prudence, we shall find the greatest advantage in making wise observations on our conduct.

senses.d: Hence: An expression of an opinion or judgment upon what one has observed; a remark.
q: To observations which ourselves we make We grow more partial for the observer's sake.

senses.d: Performance of what is prescribed; adherence in practice; observance.
q: We are to procure dispensation or leave to omit the observation of it in such circumstances.

senses.d: The act of recognizing and noting some fact or occurrence in nature, as an aurora, a corona, or the structure of an animal.

Observation.syn: Observance; notice; attention; remark; comment; note. See Observance.

senses.d: To take notice of by appropriate conduct; to conform one's action or practice to; to keep; to heed; to obey; to comply with; as, to observe rules or commands; to observe civility.
q: Ye shall observe the feast of unleavened bread.
He wolde no such cursedness observe.
Must I budge? Must I observe you?
With solemn purpose to observe Immutably his sovereign will.

senses.d: To be on the watch respecting; to pay attention to; to notice with care; to see; to perceive; to discover; as, to observe an eclipse; to observe the color or fashion of a dress; to observe the movements of an army.
To express as what has been noticed; to utter as a remark; to say in a casual or incidental way; to remark.

Observe.etym: [L. observare, observatum; ob (see Ob-) + servare to save, preserve, keep, heed, observe: cf. F. observer. See Serve.]

senses.d: To take notice; to give attention to what one sees or hears; to attend.
To make a remark; to comment; — generally with on or upon.
q: I have barely quoted . . . without observing upon it.

senses.d: One who observes, or pays attention to, anything; especially, one engaged in, or trained to habits of, close and exact observation; as, an astronomical observer.
q: The observed of all observers.
Careful observers may foretell the hour, By sure prognostic, when to dread a shower.

senses.d: One who keeps any law, custom, regulation, rite, etc.; one who conforms to anything in practice.
q: These . . . hearkened unto observers of times.

senses.d: One who fulfills or performs; as, an observer of his promises.
A sycophantic follower.
Pertinaciously adhering to an opinion, purpose, or course; persistent; not yielding to reason, arguments, or other means; stubborn; pertinacious; — usually implying unreasonableness.
q: I have known great cures done by obstinate resolution of drinking no wine.
No ass so meek, no ass so obstinate.
Of sense and outward things.

senses.d: Not yielding; not easily subdued or removed; as, obstinate fever; obstinate obstructions.

Obstinate.syn: Stubborn; inflexible; immovable; firm; pertinacious; persistent; headstrong; opinionated; unyielding; refractory; contumacious. See Stubborn.
Obstinate.etym: [L. obstinatus, p. p. of obstinare to set about a thing with firmness, to persist in; ob (see Ob-) + a word from the root of stare to stand. See Stand, and cf. Destine.]

senses.d: To hold; to keep; to possess.
q: His mother, then, is mortal, but his Sire He who obtains the monarchy of heaven.

senses.d: To get hold of by effort; to gain possession of; to procure; to acquire, in any way.
q: Some pray for riches; riches they obtain.
By guileful fair words peace may be obtained.
It may be that I may obtain children by her.

Obtain.syn: To attain; gain; procure; acquire; win; earn.
Obtain.etym: [F. obtenir, L. obtinere; ob (see Ob-) + tenere to hold. See Tenable.]

senses.d: To become held; to gain or have a firm footing; to be recognized or established; to subsist; to become prevalent or general; to prevail; as, the custom obtains of going to the seashore in summer.
q: Sobriety hath by use obtained to signify temperance in drinking.
The Theodosian code, several hundred years after Justinian's time, did obtain in the western parts of Europe.

senses.d: To prevail; to succeed.
q: So run that ye may obtain.
There is due from the judge to the advocate, some commendation, where causes are fair pleaded; especially towards the side which obtaineth not.

senses.d: To gain or have a firm footing; to become recognized or established; to become or be prevalent or general; as, the custom obtains of going to the seashore in summer.
A falling out, happening, or coming to pass; hence, that which falls out or happens; occurrence; incident.
q: The unlooked-for incidents of family history, and its hidden excitements, and its arduous occasions.

senses.d: A favorable opportunity; a convenient or timely chance; convenience.
q: Sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me.
I'll take the occasion which he gives to bring Him to his death.

senses.d: An occurrence or condition of affairs which brings with it some unlooked-for event; that which incidentally brings to pass an event, without being its efficient cause or sufficient reason; accidental or incidental cause.
q: Her beauty was the occasion of the war.

senses.d: Need; exigency; requirement; necessity; as, I have no occasion for firearms.
q: After we have served ourselves and our own occasions.
When my occasions took me into France.

senses.d: A reason or excuse; a motive; a persuasion.
q: Whose manner was, all passengers to stay, And entertain with her occasions sly.

Occasion.etym: [F. occasion, L. occasio, fr. occidere, occasum, to fall down; ob (see Ob-) + cadere to fall. See Chance, and cf. Occident.]

senses.d: To give occasion to; to cause; to produce; to induce; as, to occasion anxiety.
q: If we inquire what it is that occasions men to make several combinations of simple ideas into distinct modes.

senses.d: The act or process of occupying or taking possession; actual possession and control; the state of being occupied; a holding or keeping; tenure; use; as, the occupation of lands by a tenant.
That which occupies or engages the time and attention; the principal business of one's life; vocation; employment; calling; trade.
q: Absence of occupation is not rest.

Occupation.syn: Occupancy; possession; tenure; use; employment; avocation; engagement; vocation; calling; office; trade; profession.

senses.d: One who occupies, or has possession.
One who follows an employment; hence, a tradesman.
q: The occupiers of thy merchandise.

senses.d: To take or hold possession of; to hold or keep for use; to possess.
q: Woe occupieth the fine of our gladness.
The better apartments were already occupied.

senses.d: To hold, or fill, the dimensions of; to take up the room or space of; to cover or fill; as, the camp occupies five acres of ground.
To possess or use the time or capacity of; to engage the service of; to employ; to busy.
q: An archbishop may have cause to occupy more chaplains than six.
They occupied themselves about the Sabbath.

senses.d: To do business in; to busy one's self with.
q: All the ships of the sea, with their mariners, were in thee to occupy the merchandise.
Not able to occupy their old crafts.

senses.d: To use; to expend; to make use of.
q: All the gold that was occupied for the work.
They occupy not money themselves.

senses.d: To have sexual intercourse with.

Occupy.etym: [OE. occupien, F. occuper, fr.L. occupare; ob (see Ob-) + a word akin to capere to take. See Capacious.]

senses.d: To hold possession; to be an occupant.
To follow business; to traffic.
Occurring or happening; hence, incidental; accidental.

Occurrent.etym: [L. occurrens, -entis, p. pr. of occurrere: cf. F. occurrent. See Occur.]

senses.d: One who meets; hence, an adversary.
Anything that happens; an occurrence.
q: These we must meet with in obvious occurrents of the world.

senses.d: An alleged force or natural power, supposed, by Reichenbach and others, to produce the phenomena of mesmerism, and to be developed by various agencies, as by magnets, heat, light, chemical or vital action, etc.; — called also odyle or the odylic force.
q: That od force of German Reichenbach Which still, from female finger tips, burnt blue.

senses.d: Not paired with another, or remaining over after a pairing; without a mate; unmatched; single; as, an odd shoe; an odd glove.
Not divisible by 2 without a remainder; not capable of being evenly paired, one unit with another; as, 1, 3, 7, 9, 11, etc., are odd numbers.
q: I hope good luck lies in odd numbers.

senses.d: Left over after a definite round number has been taken or mentioned; indefinitely, but not greatly, exceeding a specified number; extra.
q: Sixteen hundred and odd years after the earth was made, it was destroyed in a deluge.
There are yet missing of your company Some few odd lads that you remember not.

senses.d: Remaining over; unconnected; detached; fragmentary; hence, occasional; inconsiderable; as, odd jobs; odd minutes; odd trifles.
Different from what is usual or common; unusual; singular; peculiar; unique; strange.
q: The odd man, to perform all things perfectly, is, in my poor opinion, Joannes Sturmius.
Patients have sometimes coveted odd things.
Locke's Essay would be a very odd book for a man to make himself master of, who would get a reputation by critical writings.

Odd.syn: Quaint; unmatched; singular; unusual; extraordinary; strange; queer; eccentric; whimsical; fantastical; droll; comical. See Quaint.
Odd.etym: [OE. odde, fr. Icel. oddi a tongue of land, a triangle, an odd number (from the third or odd angle, or point, of a triangle), orig., a point, tip; akin to Icel. oddr point, point of a weapon, Sw. udda odd, udd point, Dan. od, AS. ord, OHG. ort, G. ort place (cf. E. point, for change of meaning).]

senses.d: A short poetical composition proper to be set to music or sung; a lyric poem; esp., now, a poem characterized by sustained noble sentiment and appropriate dignity of style.
q: Hangs odes upon hawthorns and elegies on brambles.
O! run; prevent them with thy humble ode, And lay it lowly at his blessed feet.

Ode.etym: [F., fr. L. ode, oda, Gr. ᾠδή a song, especially a lyric song, contr. fr. αοιδἤ, fr. αεἴδειν to sing; cf. Skr. vad to speak, sing. Cf. Comedy, Melody, Monody.]

senses.d: Hateful; deserving or receiving hatred; as, an odious name, system, vice.
q: He rendered himself odious to the Parliament.

senses.d: Causing or provoking hatred, repugnance, or disgust; offensive; disagreeable; repulsive; as, an odious sight; an odious smell.
q: The odious side of that polity.

Odious.syn: Hateful; detestable; abominable; disgusting; loathsome; invidious; repulsive; forbidding; unpopular.
Odious.etym: [L. odiosus, from odium hatred: cf. F. odieux. See Odium.]

senses.d: In a general sense, from, or out from; proceeding from; belonging to; relating to; concerning; — used in a variety of applications; as:
Denoting that from which anything proceeds; indicating origin, source, descent, and the like; as, he is of a race of kings; he is of noble blood.
q: That holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you.

senses.d: Denoting possession or ownership, or the relation of subject to attribute; as, the apartment of the consul: the power of the king; a man of courage; the gate of heaven.
Denoting the material of which anything is composed, or that which it contains; as, a throne of gold; a sword of steel; a wreath of mist; a cup of water.

Denoting part of an aggregate or whole; belonging to a number or quantity mentioned; out of; from amongst; as, of this little he had some to spare; some of the mines were unproductive; most of the company.
q: It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed.
It is a duty to communicate of those blessings we have received.

senses.d: Denoting that by which a person or thing is actuated or impelled; also, the source of a purpose or action; as, they went of their own will; no body can move of itself; he did it of necessity.
q: For it was of the Lord to harden their hearts.

senses.d: Denoting reference to a thing; about; concerning; relating to; as, to boast of one's achievements.
q: Knew you of this fair work?

senses.d: Denoting nearness or distance, either in space or time; from; as, within a league of the town; within an hour of the appointed time.
Denoting identity or equivalence; — used with a name or appellation, and equivalent to the relation of apposition; as, the continent of America; the city of Rome; the Island of Cuba.
Denoting the agent, or person by whom, or thing by which, anything is, or is done; by.
q: And told to her of some.
He taught in their synagogues, being glorified of all.
being forty days tempted of the devil.

senses.d: Denoting relation to place or time; belonging to, or connected with; as, men of Athens; the people of the Middle Ages; in the days of Herod.
Denoting passage from one state to another; from.

Of.etym: [AS. of of, from, off; akin to D. & OS. af, G. ab off, OHG. aba from, away, Icel., Dan., Sw., & Goth. af, L. ab, Gr. �, Skr. apa. Cf. Off, A- (2), Ab-, After, Epi-.]

senses.d: In a general sense, denoting from or away from; as:
Denoting distance or separation; as, the house is a mile off.
Denoting the action of removing or separating; separation; as, to take off the hat or cloak; to cut off, to pare off, to clip off, to peel off, to tear off, to march off, to fly off, and the like.
Denoting a leaving, abandonment, departure, abatement, interruption, or remission; as, the fever goes off; the pain goes off; the game is off; all bets are off.
Denoting a different direction; not on or towards: away; as, to look off.
Denoting opposition or negation.
q: The questions no way touch upon puritanism, either off or on.

Off.etym: [OE. of, orig. the same word as R. of, prep., AS. of, adv. & prep. √194. See Of.]

senses.d: Away; begone; — a command to depart.
Not on; away from; as, to be off one's legs or off the bed; two miles off the shore.

On the farther side; most distant; on the side of an animal or a team farthest from the driver when he is on foot; in the United States, the right side; as, the off horse or ox in a team, in distinction from the nigh or near horse or ox; the off leg.

Designating a time when one is not strictly attentive to business or affairs, or is absent from his post, and, hence, a time when affairs are not urgent; as, he took an off day for fishing: an off year in politics.
The side of the field that is on the right of the wicket keeper.
To strike against; to attack; to assail.
To displease; to make angry; to affront.
q: A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city.

senses.d: To be offensive to; to harm; to pain; to annoy; as, strong light offends the eye; to offend the conscience.
To transgress; to violate; to sin against.
q: Marry, sir, he hath offended the law.

senses.d: To oppose or obstruct in duty; to cause to stumble; to cause to sin or to fall.
q: Who hath you misboden or offended.
If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out . . . And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off.
Great peace have they which love thy law, and nothing shall offend them.

Offend.etym: [OF. offendre, L. offendere, offensum; ob (see Ob-) + fendere (in comp.) to thrust, dash. See Defend.]

senses.d: To transgress the moral or divine law; to commit a crime; to stumble; to sin.
q: Whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.
If it be a sin to covet honor, I am the most offending soul alive.

senses.d: To cause dislike, anger, or vexation; to displease.
q: I shall offend, either to detain or give it.

senses.d: One who offends; one who violates any law, divine or human; a wrongdoer.
q: I and my son Solomon shall be counted offenders.

senses.d: To present, as an act of worship; to immolate; to sacrifice; to present in prayer or devotion; — often with up.
q: Thou shalt offer every day a bullock for a sin offering for atonement.
A holy priesthood to offer up spiritual sacrifices.

senses.d: To bring to or before; to hold out to; to present for acceptance or rejection; as, to offer a present, or a bribe; to offer one's self in marriage.
q: I offer thee three things.

senses.d: To present in words; to proffer; to make a proposal of; to suggest; as, to offer an opinion. With the infinitive as an objective: To make an offer; to declare one's willingness; as, he offered to help me.
To attempt; to undertake.
q: All that offer to defend him.

senses.d: To bid, as a price, reward, or wages; as, to offer a guinea for a ring; to offer a salary or reward.
To put in opposition to; to manifest in an offensive way; to threaten; as, to offer violence, attack, etc.

Offer.syn: To propose; propound; move; proffer; tender; sacrifice; immolate.
Offer.etym: [OE. offren, AS. offrian to sacrifice, fr. L. offerre; ob (see OB-) + ferre to bear, bring. The English word was influenced by F. offrir to offer, of the same origin. See 1st Bear.]

senses.d: To present itself; to be at hand.
q: The occasion offers, and the youth complies.

senses.d: To make an attempt; to make an essay or a trial; — used with at.
q: He would be offering at the shepherd's voice.
I will not offer at that I can not master.

senses.d: The act of offering, bringing forward, proposing, or bidding; a proffer; a first advance.
That which is offered or brought forward; a proposal to be accepted or rejected; a sum offered; a bid.
q: When offers are disdained, and love denied.

senses.d: Attempt; endeavor; essay; as, he made an offer to catch the ball.

Offer.etym: [Cf. F. offre, fr. offrir to offer, fr. L. offerre. See Offer, v. t.]

senses.d: The act of an offerer; a proffering.
That which is offered, esp. in divine service; that which is presented as an expiation or atonement for sin, or as a free gift; a sacrifice; an oblation; as, sin offering.
q: They are polluted offerings more abhorred Than spotted livers in the sacrifice.

senses.d: A sum of money offered, as in church service; as, a missionary offering. Specif.: (Ch. of Eng.) Personal tithes payable according to custom, either at certain seasons as Christmas or Easter, or on certain occasions as marriages or christenings.
q: to the offering before her should go.

senses.d: That which a person does, either voluntarily or by appointment, for, or with reference to, others; customary duty, or a duty that arises from the relations of man to man; as, kind offices, pious offices.
q: I would I could do a good office between you.

senses.d: A special duty, trust, charge, or position, conferred by authority and for a public purpose; a position of trust or authority; as, an executive or judical office; a municipal office.
A charge or trust, of a sacred nature, conferred by God himself; as, the office of a priest under the old dispensation, and that of the apostles in the new.
q: Inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office.

senses.d: That which is performed, intended, or assigned to be done, by a particular thing, or that which anything is fitted to perform; a function; — answering to duty in intelligent beings.
q: They resign their office and their light.
Hesperus, whose office is to bring Twilight upon the earth.
In this experiment the several intervals of the teeth of the comb do the office of so many prisms.

senses.d: The place where a particular kind of business or service for others is transacted; a house or apartment in which public officers and others transact business; as, the register's office; a lawyer's office.
The company or corporation, or persons collectively, whose place of business is in an office; as, I have notified the office.
The apartments or outhouses in which the domestics discharge the duties attached to the service of a house, as kitchens, pantries, stables, etc.
q: As for the offices, let them stand at distance.

senses.d: Any service other than that of ordination and the Mass; any prescribed religious service.
q: This morning was read in the church, after the office was done, the declaration setting forth the late conspiracy against the king's person.

Office.etym: [F., fr. L. officium, for opificium; ops ability, wealth, help + facere to do or make. See Opulent, Fact.]

senses.d: To perform, as the duties of an office; to discharge.
One who holds an office; a person lawfully invested with an office, whether civil, military, or ecclesiastical; as, a church officer; a police officer; a staff officer.
Specifically, a commissioned officer, in distinction from a warrant officer.

Officer.etym: [F. officier. See Office, and cf. Official, n.]

senses.d: To furnish with officers; to appoint officers over.
To command as an officer; as, veterans from old regiments officered the recruits.
That which is scoured off; hence, refuse; rejected matter; that which is vile or despised.
The act of production; generation.
That which is produced; a child or children; a descendant or descendants, however remote from the stock.
q: To the gods alone Our future offspring and our wives are known.

senses.d: Origin; lineage; family.
Often; frequently; not rarely; many times.
q: Oft she rejects, but never once offends.

Oft.etym: [AS. oft; akin to OS. & G. oft, OHG. ofto, Sw. ofta, Dan. ofte, Icel. opt, Goth. ufta; of uncertain origin. Cf. Often.]

senses.d: Frequent; often; repeated.
Frequently; many times; not seldom.

Often.etym: [Formerly also ofte, fr. oft. See Oft., adv.]

senses.d: Frequent; common; repeated.
q: And weary thee with often welcomes.

senses.d: Frequently; often; many times.
Frequently; often.
An exclamation expressing various emotions, according to the tone and manner, especially surprise, pain, sorrow, anxiety, or a wish. See the Note under O.

Any one of a great variety of unctuous combustible substances, not miscible with water; as, olive oil, whale oil, rock oil, etc. They are of animal, vegetable, or mineral origin and of varied composition, and they are variously used for food, for solvents, for anointing, lubrication, illumination, etc. By extension, any substance of an oily consistency; as, oil of vitriol.

Oil.etym: [OE. oile, OF. oile, F. huile, fr. L. oleum; akin to Gr. �. Cf. Olive.]

senses.d: To smear or rub over with oil; to lubricate with oil; to anoint with oil.
Covered or treated with oil; dressed with, or soaked in, oil.
That which serves to anoint; any soft unctuous substance used for smearing or anointing; an unguent.

Ointment.etym: [OE. oinement, OF. oignement, fr. F. oindre to anoint, L. ungere, unguere; akin to Skr. añj, and to G. anke (in Switzerland) butter. The first t in the E. word is due to the influence of anoint. Cf. Anoint, Unguent.]

senses.d: Open country.
Not young; advanced far in years or life; having lived till toward the end of the ordinary term of living; as, an old man; an old age; an old horse; an old tree.
q: Let not old age disgrace my high desire.
The melancholy news that we grow old.

senses.d: Not new or fresh; not recently made or produced; having existed for a long time; as, old wine; an old friendship.
Formerly existing; ancient; not modern; preceding; original; as, an old law; an old custom; an old promise.
Continued in life; advanced in the course of existence; having (a certain) length of existence; — designating the age of a person or thing; as, an infant a few hours old; a cathedral centuries old.
q: And Pharaoh said unto Jacob, How old art thou?

senses.d: Long practiced; hence, skilled; experienced; cunning; as, an old offender; old in vice.
q: Vane, young in years, but in sage counsel old.

senses.d: Long cultivated; as, an old farm; old land, as opposed to new land, that is, to land lately cleared.
Worn out; weakened or exhausted by use; past usefulness; as, old shoes; old clothes.
More than enough; abundant.
q: If a man were porter of hell gate, he should have old turning the key.

senses.d: Aged; antiquated; hence, wanting in the mental vigor or other qualities belonging to youth; — used disparagingly as a term of reproach.
Old-fashioned; wonted; customary; as of old; as, the good old times; hence, colloquially, gay; jolly.
Used colloquially as a term of cordiality and familiarity.

Old.syn: Aged; ancient; pristine; primitive; antique; antiquated; old-fashioned; obsolete. See Ancient.
Old.etym: [OE. old, ald, AS. ald, eald; akin to D. oud, OS. ald, OFries. ald, old, G. alt, Goth. alpeis, and also to Goth. alan to grow up, Icel. ala to bear, produce, bring up, L. alere to nourish. Cf. Adult, Alderman, Aliment, Auld, Elder.]

senses.d: The state or quality of being old; old age.

A tree (Olea Europæa) with small oblong or elliptical leaves, axillary clusters of flowers, and oval, one-seeded drupes. The tree has been cultivated for its fruit for thousands of years, and its branches are the emblems of peace. The wood is yellowish brown and beautifully variegated.
Any shell of the genus Oliva and allied genera; — so called from the form. See Oliva.
The color of the olive, a peculiar dark brownish, yellowish, or tawny green.
An olivary body. See under Olivary.
A small slice of meat seasoned, rolled up, and cooked; as, olives of beef or veal.

Olive.etym: [F., fr. L. oliva, akin to Gr. �. See Oil.]

senses.d: Approaching the color of the olive; of a peculiar dark brownish, yellowish, or tawny green.
The last letter of the Greek alphabet. See Alpha.
The last; the end; hence, death.
q: “Omega! thou art Lord,” they said.
The alpha and omega of science.

Omega.etym: [NL., fr. Gr. ὠ̑ μέγα, i.e., the great or long o. Cf. Mickle.]

senses.d: A Hebrew measure, the tenth of an ephah. See Ephah.
To let go; to leave unmentioned; not to insert or name; to drop.
q: These personal comparisons I omit.

senses.d: To pass by; to forbear or fail to perform or to make use of; to leave undone; to neglect.
q: Her father omitted nothing in her education that might make her the most accomplished woman of her age.

Omit.etym: [L. omittere, omissum; ob (see Ob- + mittere to cause to go, let go, send. See Mission.]

senses.d: Able in every respect and for every work; unlimited in ability; all-powerful; almighty; as, the Being that can create worlds must be omnipotent.
q: God's will and pleasure and his omnipotent power.

senses.d: Having unlimited power of a particular kind; as, omnipotent love.

Omnipotent.etym: [F., fr.L. omnipotens, -entis; omnis all + potens powerful, potent. See Potent.]

senses.d: The general signification of on is situation, motion, or condition with respect to contact or support beneath

At, or in contact with, the surface or upper part of a thing, and supported by it; placed or lying in contact with the surface; as, the book lies on the table, which stands on the floor of a house on an island.
q: I stood on the bridge at midnight.

senses.d: To or against the surface of; — used to indicate the motion of a thing as coming or falling to the surface of another; as, rain falls on the earth.
q: Whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken.

senses.d: Denoting performance or action by contact with the surface, upper part, or outside of anything; hence, by means of; with; as, to play on a violin or piano. Hence, figuratively, to work on one's feelings; to make an impression on the mind.
At or near; adjacent to; — indicating situation, place, or position; as, on the one hand, on the other hand; the fleet is on the American coast.
In addition to; besides; — indicating multiplication or succession in a series; as, heaps on heaps; mischief on mischief; loss on loss; thought on thought.

Indicating dependence or reliance; with confidence in; as, to depend on a person for assistance; to rely on; hence, indicating the ground or support of anything; as, he will promise on certain conditions; to bet on a horse.
At or in the time of; during; as, on Sunday we abstain from labor. See At (synonym).

At the time of, conveying some notion of cause or motive; as, on public occasions, the officers appear in full dress or uniform. Hence, in consequence of, or following; as, on the ratification of the treaty, the armies were disbanded.
Toward; for; — indicating the object of some passion; as, have pity or compassion on him.
At the peril of, or for the safety of.
By virtue of; with the pledge of; — denoting a pledge or engagement, and put before the thing pledged; as, he affirmed or promised on his word, or on his honor.

On.etym: [OE. on, an, o, a, AS. on, an; akin to D. aan, OS. & G. an, OHG. ana, Icel. ā, Sw. å, Goth. ana, Russ. na, L. an-, in anhelare to pant, Gr. ανἄ, Zend ana. √195. Cf. A-, 1, Ana-, Anon.]

senses.d: Forward, in progression; onward; — usually with a verb of motion; as, move on; go on.
q: The path is smooth that leadeth on to danger.

senses.d: Forward, in succession; as, from father to son, from the son to the grandson, and so on.
In continuance; without interruption or ceasing; as, sleep on, take your ease; say on; sing on.
Adhering; not off; as in the phrase, “He is neither on nor off,” that is, he is not steady, he is irresolute.
Attached to the body, as clothing or ornament, or for use.
q: He put on righteousness as a breastplate.

senses.d: In progress; proceeding; as, a game is on.
The ounce.
By limitation to the number one; for one time; not twice nor any number of times more than one.
q: Ye shall . . . go round about the city once.
Trees that bear mast are fruitful but once in two years.

senses.d: At some one period of time; — used indefinitely.
q: My soul had once some foolish fondness for thee.
That court which we shall once govern.

senses.d: At any one time; — often nearly equivalent to ever, if ever, or whenever; as, once kindled, it may not be quenched.
q: Wilt thou not be made clean? When shall it once be?
To be once in doubt Is once to be resolved.

Once.etym: [OE. ones, anes, an adverbial form fr. one, on, an, one. See One-, -Wards.]

senses.d: Being a single unit, or entire being or thing, and no more; not multifold; single; individual.
q: The dream of Pharaoh is one.
O that we now had here But one ten thousand of those men in England.

senses.d: Denoting a person or thing conceived or spoken of indefinitely; a certain. “I am the sister of one Claudio” [Shak.], that is, of a certain man named Claudio.
Pointing out a contrast, or denoting a particular thing or person different from some other specified; — used as a correlative adjective, with or without the.
q: From the one side of heaven unto the other.

senses.d: Closely bound together; undivided; united; constituting a whole.
q: The church is therefore one, though the members may be many.

senses.d: Single in kind; the same; a common.
q: One plague was on you all, and on your lords.

senses.d: Single; unmarried.
q: Men may counsel a woman to be one.

One.etym: [OE. one, on, an, AS. ān; akin to D. een, OS. ēn, OFries. ēn, ān, G. ein, Dan. een, Sw. en, Icel. einn, Goth. ains, W. un, Ir. & Gael. aon, L. unus, earlier oinos, oenos, Gr. οἴνη the ace on dice; cf. Skr. ēka. The same word as the indefinite article a, an. √ 299. Cf. 2d A, 1st An, Alone, Anon, Any,

senses.d: A single unit; as, one is the base of all numbers.
A symbol representing a unit, as 1, or i.
A single person or thing.
q: He will hate the one, and love the other.
That we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory.

senses.d: Any person, indefinitely; a person or body; as, what one would have well done, one should do one's self.
q: It was well worth one's while.
Against this sort of condemnation one must steel one's self as one best can.

senses.d: To cause to become one; to gather into a single whole; to unite; to assimilite.
q: The rich folk that embraced and oned all their heart to treasure of the world.

senses.d: Once.

A liliaceous plant of the genus Allium (A. cepa), having a strong-flavored bulb and long hollow leaves; also, its bulbous root, much used as an article of food. The name is often extended to other species of the genus.

Onion.etym: [F. ognon, fr. L. unio oneness, unity, a single large pearl, an onion. See One, Union.]

senses.d: One alone; single; as, the only man present; his only occupation.
Alone in its class; by itself; not associated with others of the same class or kind; as, an only child.
Hence, figuratively: Alone, by reason of superiority; preëminent; chief.

Only.etym: [OE. only, anly, onlich, AS. ānlic, i.e., onelike. See One, and Like, a.]

senses.d: In one manner or degree; for one purpose alone; simply; merely; barely.
q: And to be loved himself, needs only to be known.

senses.d: So and no otherwise; no other than; exclusively; solely; wholly.
q: Every imagination . . . of his heart was only evil.

senses.d: Singly; without more; as, only-begotten.
Above all others; particularly.
q: His most only elected mistress.

senses.d: Save or except (that); — an adversative used elliptically with or without that, and properly introducing a single fact or consideration.
q: He might have seemed some secretary or clerk . . . only that his low, flat, unadorned cap . . . indicated that he belonged to the city.

senses.d: Moving in a forward direction; tending toward a contemplated or desirable end; forward; as, an onward course, progress, etc.
Advanced in a forward direction or toward an end.
q: Within a while, Philoxenus came to see how onward the fruits were of his friend's labor.

senses.d: Toward a point before or in front; forward; progressively; as, to move onward.
q: Not one looks backward, onward still he goes.

senses.d: An ingredient of the Mosaic incense, probably the operculum of some kind of strombus.
The precious stone called onyx.

Onycha.etym: [NL., from L. onyx, -ychis, onyx, also, a kind of mussel, Gr. �, �. See Onyx.]

senses.d: Chalcedony in parallel layers of different shades of color. It is used for making cameos, the figure being cut in one layer with the next as a ground.

Onyx.etym: [L., fr. Gr. � a claw, finger nail, a veined gem. See Nail, and cf. Onycha.]

senses.d: Free of access; not shut up; not closed; affording unobstructed ingress or egress; not impeding or preventing passage; not locked up or covered over; — applied to passageways; as, an open door, window, road, etc.; also, to inclosed structures or objects; as, open houses, boxes, baskets, bottles, etc.; also, to means of communication or approach by water or land; as, an open harbor or roadstead.
q: Through the gate, Wide open and unguarded, Satan passed.

senses.d: Free to be used, enjoyed, visited, or the like; not private; public; unrestricted in use; as, an open library, museum, court, or other assembly; liable to the approach, trespass, or attack of any one; unprotected; exposed.
q: If Demetrius . . . have a matter against any man, the law is open and there are deputies.
The service that I truly did his life, Hath left me open to all injuries.

senses.d: Free or cleared of obstruction to progress or to view; accessible; as, an open tract; the open sea.
Not drawn together, closed, or contracted; extended; expanded; as, an open hand; open arms; an open flower; an open prospect.
q: Each, with open arms, embraced her chosen knight.

senses.d: Without reserve or false pretense; sincere; characterized by sincerity; unfeigned; frank; also, generous; liberal; bounteous; — applied to personal appearance, or character, and to the expression of thought and feeling, etc.
q: With aspect open, shall erect his head.
The Moor is of a free and open nature.
The French are always open, familiar, and talkative.

senses.d: Not concealed or secret; not hidden or disguised; exposed to view or to knowledge; revealed; apparent; as, open schemes or plans; open shame or guilt.
q: His thefts are too open.
That I may find him, and with secret gaze Or open admiration him behold.

senses.d: Not of a quality to prevent communication, as by closing water ways, blocking roads, etc.; hence, not frosty or inclement; mild; — used of the weather or the climate; as, an open season; an open winter.
Not settled or adjusted; not decided or determined; not closed or withdrawn from consideration; as, an open account; an open question; to keep an offer or opportunity open.
Free; disengaged; unappropriated; as, to keep a day open for any purpose; to be open for an engagement.
Uttered with a relatively wide opening of the articulating organs; — said of vowels; as, the än fär is open as compared with the ā in sāy.
Not closed or stopped with the finger; — said of the string of an instrument, as of a violin, when it is allowed to vibrate throughout its whole length.

Open.syn: Unclosed; uncovered; unprotected; exposed; plain; apparent; obvious; evident; public; unreserved; frank; sincere; undissembling; artless. See Candid, and Ingenuous.
Open.etym: [AS. open; akin to D. open, OS. opan, G. offan, Icel. opinn, Sw. öppen, Dan. aaben, and perh. to E. up. Cf. Up, and Ope.]

senses.d: Open or unobstructed space; clear land, without trees or obstructions; open ocean; open water.
q: Then we got into the open.

senses.d: To make or set open; to render free of access; to unclose; to unbar; to unlock; to remove any fastening or covering from; as, to open a door; to open a box; to open a room; to open a letter.
q: And all the windows of my heart I open to the day.

senses.d: To spread; to expand; as, to open the hand.
To disclose; to reveal; to interpret; to explain.
q: The king opened himself to some of his council, that he was sorry for the earl's death.
Unto thee have I opened my cause.
While he opened to us the Scriptures.

senses.d: To make known; to discover; also, to render available or accessible for settlements, trade, etc.
q: The English did adventure far for to open the North parts of America.

senses.d: To enter upon; to begin; as, to open a discussion; to open fire upon an enemy; to open trade, or correspondence; to open a case in court, or a meeting.
To loosen or make less compact; as, to open matted cotton by separating the fibers.
q: Poetry that had opened up so many delightful views into the character and condition of our “bold peasantry, their country's pride.”

senses.d: To unclose; to form a hole, breach, or gap; to be unclosed; to be parted.
q: The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram.

senses.d: To expand; to spread out; to be disclosed; as, the harbor opened to our view.
To begin; to commence; as, the stock opened at par; the battery opened upon the enemy.
To bark on scent or view of the game.
The act or process of opening; a beginning; commencement; first appearance; as, the opening of a speech.
q: The opening of your glory was like that of light.

senses.d: A place which is open; a breach; an aperture; a gap; cleft, or hole.
q: We saw him at the opening of his tent.

senses.d: Hence: A vacant place; an opportunity; as, an opening for business.
A thinly wooded space, without undergrowth, in the midst of a forest; as, oak openings.
In an open manner; publicly; not in private; without secrecy.
q: How grossly and openly do many of us contradict the precepts of the gospel by our ungodliness!

senses.d: Without reserve or disguise; plainly; evidently.
q: My love . . . shall show itself more openly.

senses.d: The act or process of operating; agency; the exertion of power, physical, mechanical, or moral.
q: The pain and sickness caused by manna are the effects of its operation on the stomach.
Speculative painting, without the assistance of manual operation, can never attain to perfection.

senses.d: The method of working; mode of action.
That which is operated or accomplished; an effect brought about in accordance with a definite plan; as, military or naval operations.
Effect produced; influence.
q: The bards . . . had great operation on the vulgar.

senses.d: Something to be done; some transformation to be made upon quantities, the transformation being indicated either by rules or symbols.
Any methodical action of the hand, or of the hand with instruments, on the human body, to produce a curative or remedial effect, as in amputation, etc.

That which is opined; a notion or conviction founded on probable evidence; belief stronger than impression, less strong than positive knowledge; settled judgment in regard to any point of knowledge or action.
q: Opinion is when the assent of the understanding is so far gained by evidence of probability, that it rather inclines to one persuasion than to another, yet not without a mixture of incertainty or doubting.
I can not put off my opinion so easily.

senses.d: The judgment or sentiment which the mind forms of persons or things; estimation.
q: I have bought golden opinions from all sorts of people.
Friendship . . . gives a man a peculiar right and claim to the good opinion of his friend.
However, I have no opinion of those things.

senses.d: Favorable estimation; hence, consideration; reputation; fame; public sentiment or esteem.
q: Thou hast redeemed thy lost opinion.
This gained Agricola much opinion, who . . . had made such early progress into laborious . . . enterprises.

senses.d: Obstinacy in holding to one's belief or impression; opiniativeness; conceitedness.
The formal decision, or expression of views, of a judge, an umpire, a counselor, or other party officially called upon to consider and decide upon a matter or point submitted.

Opinion.syn: Sentiment; notion; persuasion; idea; view; estimation. See Sentiment.

senses.d: To opine.
Fit or convenient time; a time or place favorable for executing a purpose; a suitable combination of conditions; suitable occasion; chance.
q: A wise man will make more opportunities than he finds.

senses.d: Convenience of situation; fitness.
q: Hull, a town of great strength and opportunity, both to sea and land affairs.

senses.d: Importunity; earnestness.
To place in front of, or over against; to set opposite; to exhibit.
q: Her grace sat down . . . In a rich chair of state; opposing freely The beauty of her person to the people.

senses.d: To put in opposition, with a view to counterbalance or countervail; to set against; to offer antagonistically.
q: I may . . . oppose my single opinion to his.

senses.d: To resist or antagonize by physical means, or by arguments, etc.; to contend against; to confront; to resist; to withstand; as, to oppose the king in battle; to oppose a bill in Congress.
To compete with; to strive against; as, to oppose a rival for a prize.
q: I am . . . too weak To oppose your cunning.

Oppose.syn: To combat; withstand; contradict; deny; gainsay; oppugn; contravene; check; obstruct.
Oppose.etym: [F. opposer. See Ob-, Pose, and cf.2d Appose, Puzzle, n. Cf.L. opponere, oppositum.]

senses.d: To be set opposite.
To act adversely or in opposition; — with against or to; as, a servant opposed against the act.
To make objection or opposition in controversy.
The act of opposing; an attempt to check, restrain, or defeat; resistance.
q: The counterpoise of so great an opposition.
Virtue which breaks through all opposition.

senses.d: The state of being placed over against; situation so as to front something else.
Repugnance; contrariety of sentiment, interest, or purpose; antipathy.
That which opposes; an obstacle; specifically, the aggregate of persons or things opposing; hence, in politics and parliamentary practice, the party opposed to the party in power.

The situation of a heavenly body with respect to another when in the part of the heavens directly opposite to it; especially, the position of a planet or satellite when its longitude differs from that of the sun 180°; — signified by the symbol �; as, � ♃ ☉, opposition of Jupiter to the sun.

The relation between two propositions when, having the same subject and predicate, they differ in quantity, or in quality, or in both; or between two propositions which have the same matter but a different form.
To impose excessive burdens upon; to overload; hence, to treat with unjust rigor or with cruelty.
q: For thee, oppressèd king, am I cast down.
Behold the kings of the earth; how they oppress Thy chosen !

senses.d: To ravish; to violate.
To put down; to crush out; to suppress.
q: The mutiny he there hastes to oppress.

senses.d: To produce a sensation of weight in (some part of the body); as, my lungs are oppressed by the damp air; excess of food oppresses the stomach.

Oppress.etym: [F. oppresser, LL. oppressare, fr. L. oppressus, p. p. of opprimere; ob (see Ob-) + premere to press. See Press.]

senses.d: The act of oppressing, or state of being oppressed.
That which oppresses; a hardship or injustice; cruelty; severity; tyranny.
A sense of heaviness or obstruction in the body or mind; depression; dullness; lassitude; as, an oppression of spirits; an oppression of the lungs.
q: There gentle Sleep First found me, and with soft oppression seized My drowsed sense.

senses.d: Ravishment; rape.
One who oppresses; one who imposes unjust burdens on others; one who harasses others with unjust laws or unreasonable severity.
q: The orphan pines while the oppressor feeds.
To relieve the oppressed and to punish the oppressor.

senses.d: A particle that marks an alternative; as, you may read or may write, — that is, you may do one of the things at your pleasure, but not both. It corresponds to either. You may ride either to London or to Windsor. It often connects a series of words or propositions, presenting a choice of either; as, he may study law, or medicine, or divinity, or he may enter into trade.
q: If man's convenience, health, Or safety interfere, his rights and claims Are paramount.

Or.etym: [OE. or, outher, other, auther, either, or, AS. āwðer, contr. from āhwæðer; ā aye + hwæðer whether. See Aye, and Whether, and cf. Either.]

senses.d: Ere; before; sooner than.
q: But natheless, while I have time and space, Or that I forther in this tale pace.

Or.etym: [AS. �r ere, before. √204. See Ere, prep. & adv.]

senses.d: Yellow or gold color, — represented in drawing or engraving by small dots.

Or.etym: [F., fr. L. aurum gold. Cf. Aureate.]

senses.d: The answer of a god, or some person reputed to be a god, to an inquiry respecting some affair or future event, as the success of an enterprise or battle.
q: Whatso'er she saith, for oracles must stand.

senses.d: Hence: The deity who was supposed to give the answer; also, the place where it was given.
q: The oracles are dumb; No voice or hideous hum Runs through the arched roof in words deceiving.

senses.d: The communications, revelations, or messages delivered by God to the prophets; also, the entire sacred Scriptures — usually in the plural.
q: The first principles of the oracles of God.

senses.d: The sanctuary, or Most Holy place in the temple; also, the temple itself.
q: Siloa's brook, that flow'd Fast by the oracle of God.

senses.d: One who communicates a divine command; an angel; a prophet.
q: God hath now sent his living oracle Into the world to teach his final will.

senses.d: Any person reputed uncommonly wise; one whose decisions are regarded as of great authority; as, a literary oracle.
q: The country rectors . . . thought him an oracle on points of learning.

senses.d: A wise sentence or decision of great authority.

Oracle.etym: [F., fr. L. oraculum, fr. orare to speak, utter, pray, fr. os, oris, mouth. See Oral.]

senses.d: To utter oracles.

An elaborate discourse, delivered in public, treating an important subject in a formal and dignified manner; especially, a discourse having reference to some special occasion, as a funeral, an anniversary, a celebration, or the like; — distinguished from an argument in court, a popular harangue, a sermon, a lecture, etc.; as, Webster's oration at Bunker Hill.
q: The lord archbishop . . . made a long oration.

Oration.etym: [L. oratio, fr. orare to speak, utter, pray. See Oral, Orison.]

senses.d: To deliver an oration.
A public speaker; one who delivers an oration; especially, one distinguished for his skill and power as a public speaker; one who is eloquent.
q: I am no orator, as Brutus is.
Some orator renowned In Athens or free Rome.

senses.d: In equity proceedings, one who prays for relief; a petitioner.

An officer who is the voice of the university upon all public occasions, who writes, reads, and records all letters of a public nature, presents, with an appropriate address, those persons on whom honorary degrees are to be conferred, and performs other like duties; — called also public orator.

Orator.etym: [L., fr. orare to speak, utter. See Oration.]

senses.d: A garden.

An inclosure containing fruit trees; also, the fruit trees, collectively; — used especially of apples, peaches, pears, cherries, plums, or the like, less frequently of nutbearing trees and of sugar maple trees.

Orchard.etym: [AS. ortgeard, wyrtgeard, lit., wortyard, i.e., a yard for herbs; wyrt herb + geard yard. See Wort, Yard inclosure.]

senses.d: An edge or point; also, a beginning.
To set in order; to arrange according to rule; to regulate; to set; to establish.
q: The stake that shall be ordained on either side.

senses.d: To regulate, or establish, by appointment, decree, or law; to constitute; to decree; to appoint; to institute.
q: Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month.
And doth the power that man adores ordain Their doom ?

senses.d: To set apart for an office; to appoint.
q: Being ordained his special governor.

senses.d: To invest with ministerial or sacerdotal functions; to introduce into the office of the Christian ministry, by the laying on of hands, or other forms; to set apart by the ceremony of ordination.
q: Meletius was ordained by Arian bishops.

Ordain.etym: [OE. ordeinen, OF. ordener, F. ordonner, fr. L. ordinare, from ordo, ordinis, order. See Order, and cf. Ordinance.]

senses.d: Regular arrangement; any methodical or established succession or harmonious relation; method; system
q: The side chambers were . . . thirty in order.
Bright-harnessed angels sit in order serviceable.
Good order is the foundation of all good things.

senses.d: Right arrangement; a normal, correct, or fit condition; as, the house is in order; the machinery is out of order.
The customary mode of procedure; established system, as in the conduct of debates or the transaction of business; usage; custom; fashion.
q: And, pregnant with his grander thought, Brought the old order into doubt.

senses.d: Conformity with law or decorum; freedom from disturbance; general tranquillity; public quiet; as, to preserve order in a community or an assembly.
That which prescribes a method of procedure; a rule or regulation made by competent authority; as, the rules and orders of the senate.
q: The church hath authority to establish that for an order at one time which at another time it may abolish.

senses.d: A command; a mandate; a precept; a direction.
q: Upon this new fright, an order was made by both houses for disarming all the papists in England.

senses.d: Hence: A commission to purchase, sell, or supply goods; a direction, in writing, to pay money, to furnish supplies, to admit to a building, a place of entertainment, or the like; as, orders for blankets are large.
q: In those days were pit orders — beshrew the uncomfortable manager who abolished them.

senses.d: A number of things or persons arranged in a fixed or suitable place, or relative position; a rank; a row; a grade; especially, a rank or class in society; a group or division of men in the same social or other position; also, a distinct character, kind, or sort; as, the higher or lower orders of society; talent of a high order.
q: They are in equal order to their several ends.
Various orders various ensigns bear.
Which, to his order of mind, must have seemed little short of crime.

senses.d: A body of persons having some common honorary distinction or rule of obligation; esp., a body of religious persons or aggregate of convents living under a common rule; as, the Order of the Bath; the Franciscan order.
q: Find a barefoot brother out, One of our order, to associate me.
The venerable order of the Knights Templars.

senses.d: An ecclesiastical grade or rank, as of deacon, priest, or bishop; the office of the Christian ministry; — often used in the plural; as, to take orders, or to take holy orders, that is, to enter some grade of the ministry.

The disposition of a column and its component parts, and of the entablature resting upon it, in classical architecture; hence (as the column and entablature are the characteristic features of classical architecture) a style or manner of architectural designing.
An assemblage of genera having certain important characters in common; as, the Carnivora and Insectivora are orders of Mammalia.

Order.etym: [OE. ordre, F. ordre, fr. L. ordo, ordinis. Cf. Ordain, Ordinal.]

senses.d: To put in order; to reduce to a methodical arrangement; to arrange in a series, or with reference to an end. Hence, to regulate; to dispose; to direct; to rule.
q: To him that ordereth his conversation aright.
Warriors old with ordered spear and shield.

senses.d: To give an order to; to command; as, to order troops to advance.
To give an order for; to secure by an order; as, to order a carriage; to order groceries.
To admit to holy orders; to ordain; to receive into the ranks of the ministry.
q: These ordered folk be especially titled to God.
Persons presented to be ordered deacons.

senses.d: To give orders; to issue commands.
Disposition; distribution; management.
Conformed to order; in order; regular; as, an orderly course or plan.
Observant of order, authority, or rule; hence, obedient; quiet; peaceable; not unruly; as, orderly children; an orderly community.
Performed in good or established order; well-regulated.
Being on duty; keeping order; conveying orders.
According to due order; regularly; methodically; duly.
q: You are blunt; go to it orderly.

senses.d: A noncommissioned officer or soldier who attends a superior officer to carry his orders, or to render other service.
q: Orderlies were appointed to watch the palace.

senses.d: A street sweeper.
Orderly arrangement; preparation; provision.
q: They had made their ordinance Of victual, and of other purveyance.

senses.d: A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a statute, law, regulation, rescript, or accepted usage; an edict or decree; esp., a local law enacted by a municipal government; as, a municipal ordinance.
q: Thou wilt die by God's just ordinance.
By custom and the ordinance of times.
Walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.

senses.d: An established rite or ceremony.
Rank; order; station.
Ordnance; cannon.

Ordinance.etym: [OE. ordenance, OF. ordenance, F. ordonnance. See Ordain, and cf. Ordnance, Ordonnance.]

senses.d: According to established order; methodical; settled; regular.
Common; customary; usual.
q: Method is not less requisite in ordinary conversation that in writing.

senses.d: Of common rank, quality, or ability; not distinguished by superior excellence or beauty; hence, not distinguished in any way; commonplace; inferior; of little merit; as, men of ordinary judgment; an ordinary book.
q: An ordinary lad would have acquired little or no useful knowledge in such a way.

Ordinary.etym: [L. ordinarius, fr. ordo, ordinis, order: cf. F. ordinaire. See Order.]

senses.d: An officer who has original jurisdiction in his own right, and not by deputation.
The mass; the common run.
q: I see no more in you than in the ordinary Of nature's salework.

senses.d: That which is so common, or continued, as to be considered a settled establishment or institution.
q: Spain had no other wars save those which were grown into an ordinary.

senses.d: Anything which is in ordinary or common use.
q: Water buckets, wagons, cart wheels, plow socks, and other ordinaries.

senses.d: A dining room or eating house where a meal is prepared for all comers, at a fixed price for the meal, in distinction from one where each dish is separately charged; a table d'hôte; hence, also, the meal furnished at such a dining room.
q: All the odd words they have picked up in a coffeehouse, or a gaming ordinary, are produced as flowers of style.
He exacted a tribute for licenses to hawkers and peddlers and to ordinaries.

senses.d: A charge or bearing of simple form, one of nine or ten which are in constant use. The bend, chevron, chief, cross, fesse, pale, and saltire are uniformly admitted as ordinaries. Some authorities include bar, bend sinister, pile, and others. See Subordinary.
An instrument or medium by which some important action is performed, or an important end accomplished; as, legislatures, courts, armies, taxgatherers, etc., are organs of government.

A natural part or structure in an animal or a plant, capable of performing some special action (termed its function), which is essential to the life or well-being of the whole; as, the heart, lungs, etc., are organs of animals; the root, stem, foliage, etc., are organs of plants.
A component part performing an essential office in the working of any complex machine; as, the cylinder, valves, crank, etc., are organs of the steam engine.

A medium of communication between one person or body and another; as, the secretary of state is the organ of communication between the government and a foreign power; a newspaper is the organ of its editor, or of a party, sect, etc.

A wind instrument containing numerous pipes of various dimensions and kinds, which are filled with wind from a bellows, and played upon by means of keys similar to those of a piano, and sometimes by foot keys or pedals; — formerly used in the plural, each pipe being considered an organ.
q: The deep, majestic, solemn organs blow.

Organ.etym: [L. organum, Gr. �; akin to � work, and E. work: cf. F. organe. See Work, and cf. Orgue, Orgy.]

senses.d: To supply with an organ or organs; to fit with organs; to organize.
q: Thou art elemented and organed for other apprehensions.

senses.d: A large and bright constellation on the equator, between the stars Aldebaran and Sirius. It contains a remarkable nebula visible to the naked eye.
q: The flaming glories of Orion's belt.

Orion.etym: [L., fr. Gr. Ωρἴων, orig., a celebrated hunter in the oldest Greek mythology, after whom this constellation was named.]

senses.d: That which embellishes or adorns; that which adds grace or beauty; embellishment; decoration; adornment.
q: The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.
Like that long-buried body of the king Found lying with his urns and ornaments.

Ornament.etym: [OE. ornement, F. ornement, fr. L. ornamentum, fr. ornare to adorn.]

senses.d: To adorn; to deck; to embellish; to beautify; as, to ornament a room, or a city.
A child bereaved of both father and mother; sometimes, also, a child who has but one parent living.

Orphan.etym: [L. orphanus, Gr. �, akin to L. orbus. Cf. Orb a blank window.]

senses.d: Bereaved of parents, or (sometimes) of one parent.
To cause to become an orphan; to deprive of parents.
The lammergeir.
The young of the sea eagle or bald eagle.

Ossifrage.etym: [L. ossifraga, ossifragus, osprey, fr. ossifragus bone breaking; os, ossis, a bone + frangere, fractum, to break. See Osseous, Break, and cf. Osprey, Ossifragous.]

senses.d: A large bird of the genus Struthio, of which Struthio camelus of Africa is the best known species. It has long and very strong legs, adapted for rapid running; only two toes; a long neck, nearly bare of feathers; and short wings incapable of flight. The adult male is about eight feet high.

Ostrich.etym: [OE. ostriche, ostrice, OF. ostruche, ostruce, F. autruche, L. avis struthio; avis bird + struthio ostrich, fr. Gr. �, fr. � bird, sparrow. Cf. Aviary, Struthious.]

senses.d: Either; — used with other or or for its correlative (as either . . . or are now used).
q: Other of chalk, other of glass.

senses.d: Different from that which, or the one who, has been specified; not the same; not identical; additional; second of two.
q: Each of them made other for to win.
Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.

senses.d: Not this, but the contrary; opposite; as, the other side of a river.
Alternate; second; — used esp. in connection with every; as, every other day, that is, each alternate day, every second day.
Left, as opposed to right.
q: A distaff in her other hand she had.

Other.etym: [AS. ōðer; akin to OS. āðar, ōðar, D. & G. ander, OHG. andar, Icel. annarr, Sw. annan, Dan. anden, Goth. anþar, Skr. antara: cf. L. alter; all orig. comparatives: cf. Skr. anya other. √180. Cf. Alter.]

senses.d: Otherwise.
In a different manner; in another way, or in other ways; differently; contrarily.
q: Thy father was a worthy prince, And merited, alas! a better fate; But Heaven thought otherwise.

senses.d: In other respects.
q: It is said, truly, that the best men otherwise are not always the best in regard of society.

senses.d: In different circumstances; under other conditions; as, I am engaged, otherwise I would accept.
q: Let no man think me a fool; if otherwise, yet as a fool receive me.
Her eyebrows . . . rather full than otherwise.

senses.d: A socket or bezel holding a precious stone; hence, a jewel or ornament worn on the person.
q: A precious stone in a rich ouche.
Your brooches, pearls, and ouches.

Ouch.etym: [OE. ouch, nouche (a nouch being taken for an ouch: cf. Adder), fr. OF. nusche, nosche, nousche, buckle, clasp, LL. nusca, fr. OHG. nusca, nuscha.]

senses.d: Was or were under obligation to pay; owed.
q: This due obedience which they ought to the king.
The love and duty I long have ought you.
said . . . you ought him a thousand pound.

senses.d: Owned; possessed.
q: The knight the which that castle ought.

senses.d: To be bound in duty or by moral obligation.
q: We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak.

senses.d: To be necessary, fit, becoming, or expedient; to behoove; — in this sense formerly sometimes used impersonally or without a subject expressed.
q: To speak of this as it ought, would ask a volume.
Ought not Christ to have suffered these things?

Ought.etym: [Orig. the preterit of the verb to owe. OE. oughte, aughte, ahte, AS. āhte. √110. See Owe.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to us; belonging to us; as, our country; our rights; our troops; our endeavors. See I.
q: The Lord is our defense.
Our wills are ours, we know not how.

Our.etym: [AS. ūre our, of us; akin to ūs us, to us, and to G. unser our, of us, Goth. unsara. √186. See Us.]

senses.d: An emphasized form of the pronoun of the first person plural; — used as a subject, usually with we; also, alone in the predicate, in the nominative or the objective case.
q: We ourselves might distinctly number in words a great deal further then we usually do.
Safe in ourselves, while on ourselves we stand.
Unless we would denude ourself of all force.

senses.d: In its original and strict sense, out means from the interior of something; beyond the limits or boundary of somethings; in a position or relation which is exterior to something; — opposed to in or into. The something may be expressed after of, from, etc. (see Out of, below); or, if not expressed, it is implied; as, he is out; or, he is out of the house, office, business, etc.; he came out; or, he came out from the ship, meeting, sect, party, etc.
Away; abroad; off; from home, or from a certain, or a usual, place; not in; not in a particular, or a usual, place; as, the proprietor is out, his team was taken out.
q: He hath been out (of the country) nine years.

senses.d: Beyond the limits of concealment, confinement, privacy, constraint, etc., actual of figurative; hence, not in concealment, constraint, etc., in, or into, a state of freedom, openness, disclosure, publicity, etc.; as, the sun shines out; he laughed out, to be out at the elbows; the secret has leaked out, or is out; the disease broke out on his face; the book is out.
q: Leaves are out and perfect in a month.
She has not been out very long.

senses.d: Beyond the limit of existence, continuance, or supply; to the end; completely; hence, in, or into, a condition of extinction, exhaustion, completion; as, the fuel, or the fire, has burned out.
q: Deceitiful men shall not live out half their days.
When the butt is out, we will drink water.

senses.d: Beyond possession, control, or occupation; hence, in, or into, a state of want, loss, or deprivation; — used of office, business, property, knowledge, etc.; as, the Democrats went out and the Whigs came in; he put his money out at interest.
q: I have forgot my part, and I am out.

senses.d: Beyond the bounds of what is true, reasonable, correct, proper, common, etc.; in error or mistake; in a wrong or incorrect position or opinion; in a state of disagreement, opposition, etc.; in an inharmonious relation.
q: Wicked men are strangely out in the calculating of their own interest.
Very seldom out, in these his guesses.

senses.d: Not in the position to score in playing a game; not in the state or turn of the play for counting or gaining scores.

Out.etym: [OE. out, ut, oute, ute, AS. ūt, and ūte, ūtan, fr. ūt; akin to D. uit, OS. ūt, G. aus, OHG. ūz, Icel. ūt, Sw. ut, Dan. ud, Goth. ut, Skr. ud. √198. Cf. About, But, prep., Carouse, Utter, a.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, is out; especially, one who is out of office; — generally in the plural.
A place or space outside of something; a nook or corner; an angle projecting outward; an open space; — chiefly used in the phrase ins and outs; as, the ins and outs of a question. See under In.
A word or words omitted by the compositor in setting up copy; an omission.
To cause to be out; to eject; to expel.
q: A king outed from his country.
The French have been outed of their holds.

senses.d: To come out with; to make known.
To give out; to dispose of; to sell.
To come or go out; to get out or away; to become public.
Expressing impatience, anger, a desire to be rid of; — with the force of command; go out; begone; away; off.
q: Out, idle words, servants to shallow fools !

senses.d: Cast out; degraded.
One who is cast out or expelled; an exile; one driven from home, society, or country; hence, often, a degraded person; a vagabond.
q: The Lord . . . gathereth together the outcasts of Israel.

senses.d: A quarrel; a contention.

Being on the outside; external; farthest or farther from the interior, from a given station, or from any space or position regarded as a center or starting place; — opposed to inner; as, the outer wall; the outer court or gate; the outer stump in cricket; the outer world.

Outer.etym: [AS. ūtor, compar. of ūt, adv., out. See Out, Utter, a.]

senses.d: The part of a target which is beyond the circles surrounding the bull's-eye.
A shot which strikes the outer of a target.
One who puts out, ousts, or expels; also, an ouster; dispossession.
The act or the state of going out.
q: The outgoings of the morning and evening.

senses.d: That which goes out; outgo; outlay.
The extreme limit; the place of ending.
q: The outgoings of the border were at the north bay of the salt sea, at the south end of Jordan.

senses.d: Going out; departing; as, the outgoing administration; an outgoing steamer.
Foreign; not native.
q: Him did outlandish women cause to sin.
Its barley water and its outlandish wines.

senses.d: Hence: Not according with usage; strange; rude; barbarous; uncouth; clownish; as, an outlandish dress, behavior, or speech.
q: Something outlandish, unearthy, or at variance with ordinary fashion.

Outlandish.etym: [AS. ūtlendisc foreign. See Out, Land, and -ish.]

senses.d: To live beyond, or longer than; to survive.
q: They live too long who happiness outlive.

senses.d: Farthest from the middle or interior; farthest outward; outermost.

Outmost.etym: [OE. outemest, utmest, AS. ūtemest, a superl. fr. ūte out. See Out, Utmost, and cf. Outermost.]

senses.d: Of the nature of an outrage; exceeding the limits of right, reason, or decency; involving or doing an outrage; furious; violent; atrocious.

Outrageous.syn: Violent; furious; exorbitant; excessive; atrocious; monstrous; wanton; nefarious; heinous.
Outrageous.etym: [OF. outrageus, F. outrageux. See Outrage, n.]

senses.d: To exceed, or leave behind, in running; to run faster than; to outstrip; to go beyond.
q: Your zeal outruns my wishes.
The other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulcher.

senses.d: The external part of a thing; the part, end, or side which forms the surface; that which appears, or is manifest; that which is superficial; the exterior.
q: There may be great need of an outside where there is little or nothing within.
Created beings see nothing but our outside.

senses.d: The part or space which lies without an inclosure; the outer side, as of a door, walk, or boundary.
q: I threw open the door of my chamber, and found the family standing on the outside.

senses.d: The furthest limit, as to number, quantity, extent, etc.; the utmost; as, it may last a week at the outside.
One who, or that which, is without; hence, an outside passenger, as distinguished from one who is inside. See Inside, n. 3.
Of or pertaining to the outside; external; exterior; superficial.
Reaching the extreme or farthest limit, as to extent, quantity, etc.; as, an outside estimate.
On or to the outside (of); without; on the exterior; as, to ride outside the coach; he stayed outside.
To stretch out.
From the interior part; in a direction from the interior toward the exterior; out; to the outside; beyond; off; away; as, a ship bound outward.
q: The wrong side may be turned outward.
Light falling on them is not reflected outwards.

senses.d: Forming the superficial part; external; exterior; — opposed to inward; as, an outward garment or layer.
q: Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
