senses.d: Of or pertaining to the outer surface or to what is external; manifest; public.
q: An outward honor for an inward toil.

senses.d: Foreign; not civil or intestine; as, an outward war.
Tending to the exterior or outside.
q: The fire will force its outward way.

senses.d: External form; exterior.
q: So fair an outward and such stuff within.

senses.d: A place arched over with brick or stonework, and used for baking, heating, or drying; hence, any structure, whether fixed or portable, which may be heated for baking, drying, etc.; esp., now, a chamber in a stove, used for baking or roasting.

Oven.etym: [AS. ofen; akin to D. oven, OHG. ofan, ovan, G. ofen, Icel. ofn, Dan. ovn, Sw. ugn, Goth. aúhns, Gr. ιπνὄσ, Skr. ukhā pot.]

senses.d: Above, or higher than, in place or position, with the idea of covering; — opposed to under; as, clouds are over our heads; the smoke rises over the city.
q: The mercy seat that is over the testimony.
Over them gleamed far off the crimson banners of morning.

senses.d: Across; from side to side of; — implying a passing or moving, either above the substance or thing, or on the surface of it; as, a dog leaps over a stream or a table.
q: Certain lakes . . . poison birds which fly over them.

senses.d: Upon the surface of, or the whole surface of; hither and thither upon; throughout the whole extent of; as, to wander over the earth; to walk over a field, or over a city.
Above; — implying superiority in excellence, dignity, condition, or value; as, the advantages which the Christian world has over the heathen.
Above in authority or station; — implying government, direction, care, attention, guard, responsibility, etc.; — opposed to under.
q: Thou shalt be over my house.
I will make thee rules over many things.
Dost thou not watch over my sin ?
His tender mercies are over all his works.

senses.d: Across or during the time of; from beginning to end of; as, to keep anything over night; to keep corn over winter.
Above the perpendicular height or length of, with an idea of measurement; as, the water, or the depth of water, was over his head, over his shoes.
Beyond; in excess of; in addition to; more than; as, it cost over five dollars.
Above, implying superiority after a contest; in spite of; notwithstanding; as, he triumphed over difficulties; the bill was passed over the veto.

Over.etym: [AS. ofer; akin to D. over, G. über, OHG. ubir, ubar, Dan. over, Sw. öfver, Icel. yfir, Goth. ufar, L. super, Gr. υπἕρ, Skr. upari. √199. Cf. Above, Eaves, Hyper-, Orlop, Super-, Sovereign, Up.]

senses.d: From one side to another; from side to side; across; crosswise; as, a board, or a tree, a foot over, i.e., a foot in diameter.
From one person or place to another regarded as on the opposite side of a space or barrier; — used with verbs of motion; as, to sail over to England; to hand over the money; to go over to the enemy.
From beginning to end; throughout the course, extent, or expanse of anything; as, to look over accounts, or a stock of goods; a dress covered over with jewels.
From inside to outside, above or across the brim.
q: Good measure, pressed down . . . and running over.

senses.d: Beyond a limit; hence, in excessive degree or quantity; superfluously; with repetition; as, to do the whole work over.
q: He that gathered much had nothing over.

senses.d: In a manner to bring the under side to or towards the top; as, to turn (one's self) over; to roll a stone over; to turn over the leaves; to tip over a cart.
At an end; beyond the limit of continuance; completed; finished.
Upper; covering; higher; superior; also, excessive; too much or too great; — chiefly used in composition; as, overshoes, overcoat, over-garment, overlord, overwork, overhaste.
A certain number of balls (usually four) delivered successively from behind one wicket, after which the ball is bowled from behind the other wicket as many times, the fielders changing places.
To charge or load too heavily; to burden; to oppress; to cloy.
To fill too full; to crowd.
q: Our language is overcharged with consonants.

senses.d: To charge excessively; to charge beyond a fair rate or price.
To exaggerate; as, to overcharge a description.
To make excessive charges.
An excessive load or burden.
An excessive charge in an account.
To get the better of; to surmount; to conquer; to subdue; as, to overcome enemies in battle.
q: This wretched woman overcome Of anguish, rather than of crime, hath been.

senses.d: To overflow; to surcharge.
To come or pass over; to spread over.
q: And overcome us like a summer's cloud.

Overcome.syn: To conquer; subdue; vanquish; overpower; overthrow; overturn; defeat; crush; overbear; overwhelm; prostrate; beat; surmount. See Conquer.
Overcome.etym: [AS. ofercuman. See Over, Come, and cf. Supervene.]

senses.d: To gain the superiority; to be victorious.
To drive too hard, or far, or beyond strength.
To flow over; to cover woth, or as with, water or other fluid; to spread over; to inundate; to overwhelm.
q: The northern nations overflowed all Christendom.

senses.d: To flow over the brim of; to fill more than full.
To run over the bounds.
To be superabundant; to abound.
A flowing over, as of water or other fluid; an inundation.
That which flows over; a superfluous portion; a superabundance.
An outlet for the escape of surplus liquid.
An overflow; that which overflows; exuberance; copiousness.
q: He was ready to bestow the overflowings of his full mind on anybody who would start a subject.

senses.d: To lay, or spread, something over or across; hence, to cover; to overwhelm; to press excessively upon.
q: When any country is overlaid by the multitude which live upon it.
As when a cloud his beams doth overlay.
Framed of cedar overlaid with gold.
And overlay With this portentous bridge the dark abyss.

senses.d: To smother with a close covering, or by lying upon.
q: This woman's child died in the night; because she overlaid it.
A heap of ashes that o'erlays your fire.

senses.d: To put an overlay on.
A covering.
A piece of paper pasted upon the tympan sheet to improve the impression by making it stronger at a particular place.
A superficial covering; a coating.
To outlive.
q: The culture of Northumbria overlived the term of its political supermacy.

senses.d: To live too long, too luxuriously, or too actively.
Too much.
In too great a degree; too much.
An excess; a surplus.
To go over or beyond; to cross; as, to overpass a river; to overpass limits.
To pass over; to omit; to overlook; to disregard.
q: All the beauties of the East He slightly viewed and slightly overpassed.

senses.d: To surpass; to excel.
To pass over, away, or off.
That which remains after a supply, or beyond a quantity proposed; surplus.

Overplus.etym: [Over + L. plus more. See Plus, and cf. Surplus.]

senses.d: To run over; to grow or spread over in excess; to invade and occupy; to take possession of; as, the vine overran its trellis; the farm is overrun with witch grass.
q: Those barbarous nations that overran the world.

senses.d: To exceed in distance or speed of running; to go beyond or pass in running.
q: Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi.

senses.d: To go beyond; to extend in part beyond; as, one line overruns another in length.
To abuse or oppress, as if by treading upon.
q: None of them the feeble overran.

senses.d: To carry over, or back, as type, from one line or page into the next after, or next before.
To run, pass, spread, or flow over or by something; to be beyond, or in excess.
q: Despised and trodden down of all that overran.

senses.d: To extend beyond its due or desired length; as, a line, or advertisement, overruns.
To superintend; to watch over; to direct; to look or see after; to overlook.
To omit or neglect seeing.

Oversee.etym: [AS. oferséon to survey, to despise. See Over, and See.]

senses.d: To see too or too much; hence, to be deceived.
q: The most expert gamesters may sometimes oversee.
Your partiality to me is much overseen, if you think me fit to correct your Latin.

senses.d: One who oversees; a superintendent; a supervisor; as, an overseer of a mill; specifically, one or certain public officers; as, an overseer of the poor; an overseer of highways.
To throw a shadow, or shade, over; to darken; to obscure.
q: There was a cloud that overshadowed them.

senses.d: Fig.: To cover with a superior influence.
Watchful care; superintendence; general supervision.
An overlooking; an omission; an error.
Escape from an overlooked peril.

Oversight.syn: Superintendence; supervision; inspection; overlooking; inadvertence; neglect; mistake; error; omission.

senses.d: To spread over; to cover; as, the deluge overspread the earth.
q: Those nations of the North Which overspread the world.

senses.d: To be spread or scattered over.
To come up with in a course, pursuit, progress, or motion; to catch up with.
q: Follow after the men; and when thou dost overtake them, say . . . Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good.
He had him overtaken in his flight.

senses.d: To come upon from behind; to discover; to surprise; to capture; to overcome.
q: If a man be overtaken in a fault.
I shall see The winged vengeance overtake such children.

senses.d: Hence, figuratively, in the past participle (overtaken), drunken.
To throw over; to overturn; to upset; to turn upside down.
q: His wife overthrew the table.

senses.d: To cause to fall or to fail; to subvert; to defeat; to make a ruin of; to destroy.
q: When the walls of Thebes he overthrew.
that seeks to overthrow religion.

Overthrow.syn: To demolish; overturn; prostrate; destroy; ruin; subvert; overcome; conquer; defeat; discomfit; vanquish; beat; rout.

senses.d: The act of overthrowing; the state of being overthrown; ruin.
q: Your sudden overthrow much rueth me.

senses.d: The act of throwing a ball too high, as over a player's head.
To turn or throw from a basis, foundation, or position; to overset; as, to overturn a carriage or a building.
To subvert; to destroy; to overthrow.
To overpower; to conquer.
The act off overturning, or the state of being overturned or subverted; overthrow; as, an overturn of parties.

To cover over completely, as by a great wave; to overflow and bury beneath; to ingulf; hence, figuratively, to immerse and bear down; to overpower; to crush; to bury; to oppress, etc., overpoweringly.
q: The sea overwhelmed their enemies.
Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me.
Foul deeds will rise, Though all the earth o'erwhelm them.
Gaza yet stands; but all her sons are fallen, All in a moment overwhelmed and fallen.

senses.d: To project or impend over threateningly.
q: His louering brows o'erwhelming his fair sight.

senses.d: To cause to surround, to cover.
The act of overwhelming.
To possess; to have, as the rightful owner; to own.
q: Thou dost here usurp The name thou ow'st not.

senses.d: To have or possess, as something derived or bestowed; to be obliged to ascribe (something to some source); to be indebted or obliged for; as, he owed his wealth to his father; he owed his victory to his lieutenants.
q: O deem thy fall not owed to man's decree.

senses.d: Hence: To have or be under an obigation to restore, pay, or render (something) in return or compensation for something received; to be indebted in the sum of; as, the subject owes allegiance; the fortunate owe assistance to the unfortunate.
q: The one ought five hundred pence, and the other fifty.
A son owes help and honor to his father.

senses.d: To have an obligation to (some one) on account of something done or received; to be indebted to; as, to owe the grocer for supplies, or a laborer for services.

Owe.etym: [OE. owen, awen, aghen, to have, own, have (to do), hence, owe, AS. āgan to have; akin to G. eigen, a., own, Icel. eiga to have, Dan. eie, Sw. äga, Goth. áigan, Skr. īç. √110. Cf. Ought, v., 2d Own, Fraught.]

senses.d: Any species of raptorial birds of the family Strigidæ. They have large eyes and ears, and a conspicuous circle of feathers around each eye. They are mostly nocturnal in their habits.
A variety of the domestic pigeon.

Owl.etym: [AS. ūle; akin to D. uil, OHG. ūwila, G. eule, Icel. ugla, Sw. ugla, Dan. ugle.]

senses.d: To pry about; to prowl.
To carry wool or sheep out of England.
Hence, to carry on any contraband trade.
To grant; to acknowledge; to admit to be true; to confess; to recognize in a particular character; as, we own that we have forfeited your love.
q: The wakeful bloodhound rose, and shook his hide; But his sagacious eye an inmate owns.

Own.etym: [OE. unnen to grant, permit, be pleased with, AS. unnan to grant; akin to OS. giunnan, G. gönnen, Icel. unna; of uncertain origin. This word has been confused with own to possess.]

senses.d: Belonging to; belonging exclusively or especially to; peculiar; — most frequently following a possessive pronoun, as my, our, thy, your, his, her, its, their, in order to emphasize or intensify the idea of property, peculiar interest, or exclusive ownership; as, my own father; my own composition; my own idea; at my own price.

Own.etym: [OE. owen, awen, auen, aughen, AS. āgen, p. p. of āgan to possess; akin to OS. ēgan, G. & D. eigen, Icel. eiginn, Sw. & Dan. egen. √110. See Owe.]

senses.d: To hold as property; to have a legal or rightful title to; to be the proprietor or possessor of; to possess; as, to own a house.

Own.etym: [OE. ohnien, ahnien, AS. āgnian, fr. āgen own, a. See Own, a.]

senses.d: One who owns; a rightful proprietor; one who has the legal or rightful title, whether he is the possessor or not.

The male of bovine quadrupeds, especially the domestic animal when castrated and grown to its full size, or nearly so. The word is also applied, as a general name, to any species of bovine animals, male and female.
q: All sheep and oxen, yea, and the beasts of the field.

Ox.etym: [AS. oxa; akin to D. os. G. ochs, ochse, OHG. ohso, Icel. oxi, Sw. & Dan. oxe, Goth. aúhsa, Skr. ukshan ox, bull; cf. Skr. uksh to sprinkle. √214. Cf. Humid, Aurochs.]

senses.d: A mystic syllable or ejaculation used by Hindus and Buddhists in religious rites, — orig. among the Hindus an exclamation of assent, like Amen, then an invocation, and later a symbol of the trinity formed by Vishnu, Siva, and Brahma.
